1030.title: trataka
1030.hook: a curtain is pulled back in a temple, and a crowd leans forward to see and be seen
1030.howItsDone: Temple-goers speak of going for darshan, the sight of the deity in the murti, which in some temples comes at set times when the curtain is opened and a lamp is offered; some practitioners of trataka use a sacred image as their point of gaze.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka as dharana you can see: the mind tied to one place. Which task did you give a post to, and how many times did you walk back? Day one thousand thirty.

Evening at a temple. A small crowd stands packed in front of a closed curtain, shoes left at the door, hands holding flowers and little plates of sweets. Bells. Then the curtain is drawn aside, the lamp is lifted, and there is the image of the deity, dressed and garlanded, eyes wide. Nobody in the crowd looks away. Some fold their hands. A grandfather lifts a small boy higher so he can see. This is darshan. And it raises a question about trataka: when the thing you gaze at is not a mark on a wall, what changes?
screen: `THE CURTAIN IS DRAWN ASIDE.` → `A CROWD LEANS IN TO SEE.` → `WHAT IF THE MARK IS SACRED?`

segments.voice: Darshan means seeing, or a sight. In temple worship it names the moment of beholding the deity in the image, the murti. People speak of going to the temple for darshan, the way someone might say they're going to visit family. And in the way some devotees describe it, darshan isn't only looking. The deity is also looking back. The worshipper sees, and is seen. That changes the gaze. In trataka on a candle, the eyes do the work, and the flame doesn't care. In darshan the eyes are meeting someone. The Bhagavad Gita has a scene about the limits of that meeting. In chapter eleven, Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his supreme form. And Krishna answers, in paraphrase: you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my power. Then the vision comes, vast and blazing, more than Arjuna can hold. So the Gita says plainly that ordinary eyes aren't enough for that kind of seeing. Something has to be given. Here's where this meets the practice. Some who practice trataka choose a sacred image as their point: a picture of a deity, a symbol like Om, the face of a teacher. The method stays the same. A steady gaze, a gentle return, the image held behind closed eyes. But the gaze is now also a kind of attention offered to someone. Teachers differ on this. Some keep trataka strictly to a flame or a dot, to keep it simple. Others welcome a sacred image. Patanjali, as we saw yesterday, leaves the choice open.
screen: `DARSHAN: SEEING, AND BEING SEEN.` · `THE GAZE MEETS SOMEONE.` · `ARJUNA IS GIVEN A DIVINE EYE.` · `A SACRED IMAGE AS THE POINT.` · then, large: `THE MARK LOOKS BACK.`

segments.voice: Choose your point. If you keep a sacred image, a deity, a symbol, a photo of a teacher, set it at eye level. If not, a flame or a simple mark is just as good. Rest the eyes on it softly, blinking when you need to. If it's an image that matters to you, let the gaze feel like a greeting rather than a stare. When the eyes tire, close them and hold what stays. Then look again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, its neighbor darshan, where the gaze rests on a sacred image, and the worshipper sees and is seen.
Your line: seeing and being seen. Today, when you greet someone, give them one full, unhurried look before you speak, the way you'd look at something that matters. Day one thousand thirty.

1031.title: trataka
1031.hook: no candle, no mark on the wall: the Gita puts the point of the gaze on the body itself
1031.howItsDone: In some schools of yoga, practitioners rest a soft, half-lowered gaze toward the tip of the nose or the point between the brows during meditation, following the Gita's descriptions, and some teachers call these forms of trataka.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka met its neighbor darshan: the gaze on a sacred image, seeing and being seen. When you greeted someone, did you give them one full, unhurried look? Day one thousand thirty-one.

A train late at night. The carriage is half empty, the lights are harsh, and there's nothing to look at. No candle. No picture. No mark on the wall that isn't an advertisement. A woman across the aisle sits upright with her eyes half lowered, very still, as if looking at nothing in particular, and she stays that way for three stops. Where are her eyes? Trataka so far has needed something out there to look at. The Bhagavad Gita, describing a person in meditation, puts the point of the gaze somewhere you never have to pack.
screen: `A LATE TRAIN. NOTHING TO LOOK AT.` → `EYES HALF LOWERED, VERY STILL.` → `A POINT YOU NEVER HAVE TO PACK.`

segments.voice: In chapter six, Krishna describes how a person sits to meditate. A clean place, a seat neither too high nor too low. And then the body, in paraphrase: holding the body, head and neck straight and still, gazing at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking around in any direction. That last part matters. Not looking around. The verse isn't only about where the eyes go. It's about where they don't go. In chapter five there's a second spot. Krishna describes the sage who shuts out outside contacts, fixes the gaze between the brows, and evens out the breath moving through the nostrils. The tip of the nose. The point between the brows. Two places on the body itself. Later yoga teachers give these gazes names: nasikagra drishti, the gaze at the nose tip, and bhrumadhya drishti, the gaze between the eyebrows. Some count them as forms of trataka, a trataka with no object but the body. Commentators have wondered how literally to read the first one. The teacher Shankara, in his commentary on the Gita, reads it as if looking at the tip of the nose: eyes lowered and resting, not literally crossed. What matters is that the eyes stop roaming. Here's what this adds. Trataka on a flame trains the eyes on a point outside. The Gita's gaze brings the point home. The eyes rest on something that's always with you, on a train, in a waiting room, in bed at night. Teachers add a caution: soft eyes, never strain, and stop if the eyes ache.
screen: `BODY, HEAD, NECK STRAIGHT AND STILL.` · `THE NOSE TIP, AND NOT LOOKING AROUND.` · `BETWEEN THE BROWS, BREATH EVENED OUT.` · `AS IF LOOKING: EYES LOWERED, RESTING.` · then, large: `A POINT YOU CARRY EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, with the head and neck easy and straight. Let the eyes lower, half closed, and let them rest as if looking toward the tip of the nose. No crossing, no strain. Just stop the roaming. If the eyes feel comfortable, after a while you can lift the soft gaze toward the space between the brows, eyes closed if that's easier. Notice the breath moving evenly at the nostrils. If anything aches, let the eyes simply close and rest. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, the point moves onto the body: the tip of the nose, the space between the brows.

Your line: the eyes stop roaming. Today, somewhere with nothing to look at, a ride or a long wait, lower the eyes, let them rest, and stop the roaming until something calls you back. Day one thousand thirty-one.

1032.title: trataka
1032.hook: the candle is blown out and the room goes dark: what is a steady gaze for, after that?
1032.howItsDone: Some teachers of meditation in Hindu traditions present single-pointed gazing as a beginning, with the Gita's ideal of seeing the same Self in all beings as where the steadiness leads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka moved onto the body: the Gita's gaze at the tip of the nose and between the brows. Somewhere with nothing to look at, did the eyes stop roaming? Day one thousand thirty-two.

What is a steady gaze for, once the candle is out? The sit is over. Someone leans forward and blows. A thread of smoke, the smell of wax, and the room goes dark. Then the light switch, the kitchen, the phone, the street, a crowd of things asking to be looked at. It would be easy to think the practice ended with the flame. Today, the last day of trataka, the Gita suggests where the gaze is meant to end up, and it isn't on a candle at all.
screen: `THE SIT IS OVER. THE FLAME IS OUT.` → `A CROWD OF THINGS ASKS TO BE SEEN.` → `WHERE IS THE GAZE MEANT TO END UP?`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, after the seat, the straight back, the lamp in a windless place, Krishna describes the one whose mind has become steady in yoga. In paraphrase: such a person sees the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self, and sees the same everywhere. The Sanskrit is sama-darshana: same-seeing, an even gaze. Then, in the next verse, Krishna makes it personal. Whoever sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me, I am not lost to them, and they are not lost to me. So the steady gaze isn't the end. It's a training for a different kind of seeing. On a flame, the eyes learn to stop jumping. Here, the steadiness goes out into the world. The same evenness looks at a stranger, a sister, a sparrow, someone difficult, and doesn't swing from wanting to pushing away. Two verses later, Krishna gives that evenness a heart. In paraphrase: the one who, by the measure of one's own self, sees pleasure or pain in every being as the same, that yogi is held to be the highest. Shankara reads it plainly: as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to every being. An even gaze, then, isn't a cold one. Now the road of these seven days, in one breath: a small mark, a windless lamp, eyes turned around, a mind tied to one place, a gaze that is met, a point carried on the body, and today, a gaze that stops picking favorites. One small point, and then everything. In this arc, the flame was never the goal. It was a place for the eyes to learn to be still, so they could look at the world with the same calm.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL, ALL IN THE SELF.` · `SAMA-DARSHANA: AN EVEN GAZE.` · `I AM NOT LOST TO THEM.` · `SEVEN DAYS: FROM A MARK TO THE WORLD.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL POINT, THEN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Begin with one small point, a flame or a mark, at eye level. Rest the gaze there for a little while, blinking when you need to. Then, slowly, let the gaze soften and widen, without moving the eyes, until it takes in the whole room: the wall, the floor, the light, whatever is there. Try to look at all of it with the same calm you gave the point. No favorites. If the mind starts sorting, liking this, disliking that, come back to the point, then widen again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, practiced, the Gita suggests, until the eyes can rest on everything with the same calm.

Your line: one small point, then everything. Today, choose one person you usually look past or look at with a frown, and give them, just once, the same steady look you gave the flame. Day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: the mudras
1033.hook: a signet ring pressed into warm wax leaves a shape that stays after the ring is lifted
1033.howItsDone: In hatha yoga, mudras such as mahamudra and the bandhas are learned from a teacher as whole-body practices; in meditation, worship and dance, mudras are shapes of the hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed trataka with the even gaze: one small point, then everything, seen with the same calm. Who did you give that steady look to? Today the eyes rest, and the hands begin. Day one thousand thirty-three.

A drop of red wax falls on the fold of a letter. Someone presses a ring into it, holds it there a moment, and lifts it away. The ring is gone. The shape stays: a crest, a letter, a small picture, sharp-edged in the cooling wax. Whoever opens the letter can tell whose hand sealed it, and that nobody has opened it since. That little act, pressing a shape so that it holds, is close to the heart of today's word. For the next stretch the path turns to the mudras.
screen: `WAX ON THE FOLD OF A LETTER.` → `THE RING IS LIFTED. THE SHAPE STAYS.` → `PRESSING A SHAPE SO IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, mudra can mean a seal: a stamp, a signet, the mark it leaves. It also comes to mean a sign or a gesture. In a yoga class today, the word often points to the hands: fingers touching, palms joined. That's real, and the coming days will spend time there. But the word is bigger than the hands. Open the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the same manual that described trataka, to its third chapter, and the mudras there are whole-body practices. It names them one by one. One is mahamudra, the great seal. In the text's description, in paraphrase, one heel presses in at the base of the body, the other leg stretches out, the hands take hold of the outstretched foot, and the chin is drawn down to the chest. Others in the same list are bandhas, locks: the chin drawn in at the throat, the belly drawn in and up, the root of the body gently drawn in. Another turns the body upside down. Not a finger shape among them. So why call these seals? Back to the wax. A seal does two things. It presses a shape in, and it closes something so that it stays. The hatha texts describe their mudras in the same spirit: shapes of the body that hold the breath and the attention in, rather than letting them leak away. The text also says these practices are to be learned from a teacher, and its descriptions are spare. They aren't written as do-it-yourself instructions. What the word gives us for now is a picture. Whether it's the whole body or two fingers, a mudra is a shape that holds.
screen: `MUDRA: A SEAL, A STAMP, A SIGN.` · `IN THE HATHA TEXT, THE WHOLE BODY.` · `MAHAMUDRA, AND THE LOCKS.` · `A SHAPE PRESSED IN, SO IT HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE RING LIFTS. THE SHAPE STAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, comfortable, feet on the floor or legs crossed. Rest the hands on the thighs, palms down. Stay a few breaths and notice how it feels. Then turn the palms up and stay a few breaths more. Notice what changes, if anything. Choose whichever feels steadier and let the whole body settle into that shape, like a ring pressed into wax: still, sharp-edged, unhurried. If the mind wanders, come back to the shape. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Seals: shapes of the hands or of the whole body, pressed in so that something holds.

Your line: a seal pressed into wax. Today, at one moment you want to keep, a good meal or a kind word, pause and hold your posture still for one breath, like a seal pressed into wax. Day one thousand thirty-three.

1034.title: the mudras
1034.hook: two palms pressed together at an airport arrivals gate, before the hug, before a single word
1034.howItsDone: In Hindu homes and temples, people greet one another, elders and the deity with anjali, palms joined at the chest, often with the words namaste or namaskar and a slight bow of the head.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras began as seals: shapes of the hands or the whole body, pressed in so something holds. At a moment worth keeping, did you hold still for one breath, like a seal pressed into wax? Day one thousand thirty-four.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `A SHAPE PRESSED IN, SO IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: The arrivals gate at an airport, late in the evening. A tired young man comes through the sliding doors pulling a suitcase. An older woman at the rail sees him, and before she hugs him, before she says his name, she presses her palms together in front of her chest and dips her head. He does it back. Then the hug. Two seconds, maybe less, and nobody around them notices. That small shape of the hands is a mudra, so familiar it's easy to forget it is one.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE, LATE.` → `PALMS TOGETHER, A DIP OF THE HEAD.` → `A MUDRA, HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The gesture has a name: anjali. Two palms joined, fingers pointing up, usually held at the chest, sometimes at the forehead, sometimes raised above the head. Anjali can also mean the cupped hollow of two hands, the shape you'd make to carry water or flowers as an offering. So the joined palms carry a sense of offering. What about namaste? That's not the gesture. It's the words said with it. Namas means a bow, homage. Te means to you. Namaste: a bow to you. The hands make the shape, the voice names it, and often, as at the airport, the hands do it alone. Now watch the Bhagavad Gita use this mudra at its most overwhelming moment. In chapter eleven, Arjuna has been given the divine eye and sees Krishna's universal form, vast, blazing, with many faces and eyes. And the text tells us what his body does. In paraphrase: filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head, joined his palms, and spoke. A little later, trembling, palms still joined, he bows again and speaks in a choking voice. Then come his words: bowing to Krishna in front, behind, on every side. Notice what the text chooses to show. Not Arjuna's thoughts first. His hands. When there are no adequate words, the hands go first. And anjali travels far beyond that battlefield. It works at a temple, before an elder, to greet a guest, to say thank you or sorry. It needs no shared language. And it says something before the voice can: I bow to you.
screen: `ANJALI: PALMS JOINED, AN OFFERING.` · `NAMASTE: THE WORDS. A BOW TO YOU.` · `ARJUNA, AMAZED, JOINS HIS PALMS.` · `WHEN WORDS FAIL, THE HANDS GO FIRST.` · then, large: `I BOW TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring the palms together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, the thumbs resting lightly near the breastbone. Not pressing hard, just touching. Let the head dip a little. Feel the warmth where the two hands meet. Bring to mind someone you'd like to greet with respect, someone near or far. Hold the gesture toward them for a few breaths. If the arms tire, let the hands rest in the lap and keep the feeling. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, anjali: two palms joined, the shape of offering, and the gesture that says a bow to you before a word is spoken.
Your line: a bow to you. Today, once, when thanks or respect is due and words feel too small, let your hands say it first, palms together, a small dip of the head. Day one thousand thirty-four.

1035.title: the mudras
1035.hook: under a banyan tree, old students sit before a young teacher who says nothing, and their doubts are gone
1035.howItsDone: Practitioners sit in meditation with chin or jnana mudra, thumb and index finger touching and the hands resting on the knees; images of Dakshinamurti show him seated beneath a banyan tree with his hand in this mudra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras and anjali: palms joined, the shape of offering, a bow to you. When words felt too small, did your hands say it first? Day one thousand thirty-five.

How strange, an old Sanskrit verse begins. Under a banyan tree sit the students, and they are old. Their teacher is young. And the teacher's lecture is silence. Yet the students' doubts are cut away. The teacher in that verse is Dakshinamurti, Shiva as the teacher. In images of him beneath the tree, one hand is raised, and in that hand the thumb and the first finger touch to make a small circle. He doesn't explain it. In the verse, the silence is enough. Today, the mudra that does the teaching.
screen: `OLD STUDENTS. A YOUNG TEACHER.` → `THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.` → `ONE HAND, A SMALL CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: The shape is simple. The tip of the index finger meets the tip of the thumb. The other three fingers stay straight, relaxed. It's called chin mudra, the seal of consciousness, or jnana mudra, the seal of knowledge. Lineages use the two names a little differently, sometimes by whether the palm faces up or down, but the finger shape is the same. Teachers read the shape like a sentence. One common reading goes like this. The thumb stands for the Supreme, Brahman. The index finger, the one we point with, stands for the individual self, the one always pointing outward at this and that. When the index finger bends and touches the thumb, the small self meets the great one. And the three fingers left standing? Some teachers say they are the three gunas, the qualities that make up the world. Others say they are the three states this path spent time with not long ago: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. Either way, in that reading the circle is made apart from the three, and the meeting happens beyond them. That's why it suits Dakshinamurti. Some readers say the students are old because they've studied everything and heard every argument. What finally answers them isn't another argument. It's a hand, held still, showing the meeting instead of describing it. The Taittiriya Upanishad says something similar about its own subject: it's where words turn back, unable to reach it. Silence and a sign, then. In the verse's picture, that isn't because there's nothing to say, but because this is something better shown. And the hand can show it in a meditation seat, palm resting on the knee, as easily as it does under a banyan tree.
screen: `THUMB AND FIRST FINGER MEET.` · `THE SMALL SELF BENDS TO THE GREAT.` · `THREE FINGERS: GUNAS, OR THREE STATES.` · `SHOWN, NOT DESCRIBED.` · then, large: `THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and rest the backs of the hands on the knees or thighs. Let the tip of each index finger meet the tip of the thumb, lightly, just touching. Let the other three fingers stay straight but soft. Feel the small circle on each side. Now let the breath settle and say nothing, even inside. If thoughts start explaining, let them go and come back to the touch of the two fingertips. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, chin mudra, the seal of consciousness: thumb and first finger joined, read by teachers as the small self bowing to the great, shown in silence.

Your line: a lecture made of silence. Today, once, in a conversation where you're tempted to explain one more time, try saying less, and let a small gesture carry the rest. Day one thousand thirty-five.

1036.title: the mudras
1036.hook: a right hand with two fingers folded down, resting at the nose, opening one side and closing the other
1036.carry: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other
1036.howItsDone: In hatha yoga, practitioners do alternate-nostril breathing with the right hand, folding the first two fingers and using the thumb and ring finger to close each side in turn; breath retention is learned from a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras and the silent teacher: thumb and first finger joined in chin mudra, a lecture made of silence. In a conversation, did you say less and let a gesture carry the rest? Today closes the week. Day one thousand thirty-six.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `CHIN MUDRA: THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: A right hand, lifted to the face. The first two fingers are folded down into the palm. The thumb rests against one side of the nose, the ring finger against the other. Someone sitting very straight, eyes closed, presses gently with the thumb, and the breath goes in through the left side only. Then the ring finger closes the left, the thumb lifts, and the breath goes out through the right. Back and forth, slow as a tide. So far this week's mudras have greeted, offered and taught. Today, a mudra with a job: it steers the breath.
screen: `TWO FINGERS FOLDED DOWN.` → `THUMB ON ONE SIDE, RING FINGER ON THE OTHER.` → `A MUDRA THAT STEERS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The practice is alternate-nostril breathing, and the Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes it in its second chapter, in paraphrase: breathe in through the left nostril, then out through the right. Breathe in through the right, then out through the left. The text calls the channels of the subtle body nadis, and says this is how they're made clean. The text's version also holds the breath between in and out, which teachers say to learn in person. The hand shape isn't spelled out in that passage. Teachers supply it, and in some lineages it's called Vishnu mudra: the index and middle fingers folded down, the thumb and ring finger free to open and close the two sides. Others rest those two fingers on the brow instead. Either way, the hand becomes a valve. It's a different kind of mudra from the ones earlier this week. Anjali says something to someone. Chin mudra shows something in silence. This one does something. It's a seal in the most practical sense, closing one side so the breath has only one way to go. Now look back at the week. Darshan, the gaze that meets the deity and is met. The Gita's gaze at the tip of the nose, a point you carry everywhere. The even gaze, seeing the same in all. Then the hands took over. The mudra as a seal, a shape pressed in so it holds. Anjali, the joined palms, a bow to you. Chin mudra, the small self bending to the great, under a banyan tree. And today, the breathing hand. The eyes learned to rest. The hands learned to speak, and now to steer.
screen: `IN THROUGH ONE SIDE, OUT THROUGH THE OTHER.` · `FINGERS FOLDED, THUMB AND RING FINGER FREE.` · `A MUDRA THAT DOES SOMETHING.` · `THIS WEEK: EYES TO REST, HANDS TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `THE HAND BECOMES A VALVE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright. Fold the first two fingers of the right hand into the palm. Close the right nostril gently with the thumb and breathe in, slowly, through the left. Close the left with the ring finger, lift the thumb, and breathe out through the right. Breathe in through the right. Close it, open the left, breathe out through the left. That's one round. Keep it slow and easy, no holding, no forcing. If the nose is blocked or anything feels uncomfortable, simply rest the hand and breathe normally. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, the thumb and ring finger opening one side and closing the other.

Your line: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Today, notice once what your hands are saying without a word, clenched, open, folded, busy, and let them say something gentler. Day one thousand thirty-six.

fork.setup: your right hand is at your nose, two fingers folded. you've breathed in through the left. what comes next?
options: breathe out through the left again.
close the left and breathe out through the right.
breathe out through the mouth.
fork.reveal: the text describes in through the left, out through the right, then in through the right and out through the left.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: nadi, a channel. In hatha yoga, the channels of the subtle body that alternate-nostril breathing is said to clean.

trapdoor: what you thought: mudras are only symbols.
what it means: some mudras do a job, like the hand that steers the breath from side to side.
what a scholar hears: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.7–2.10 on nāḍī-śodhana, with the hand shape supplied by later teachers.
